planting.note: Mount on cork bark, live oak branches, or driftwood in bright indirect to gentle direct light; needs no soil. Potbelly airplant is native to Florida hammocks and the Everglades and tolerates the Gulf Coast's heat and humidity better than many showier tillandsias.

directions: Mount on bark, a tree branch, or in a hanging wire basket in bright, filtered light to a few hours of gentle morning sun. Tillandsia paucifolia is a Florida-native air plant found growing epiphytically on live oaks, cypress, and buttonwood throughout the peninsula and the Keys, forming a bulbous, swollen leaf base (hence 'potbelly') that tapers into narrow, curling gray-green leaves. Clusters of tubular lavender-blue flowers emerge from a pink-bracted inflorescence, typically in spring. It is one of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant tillandsias for Gulf Coast outdoor mounting, handling brief cold snaps into the upper 20s F once established. Water by misting or dunking two to three times a week in summer, less in winter, and shake out any water trapped in the leaf axils to prevent rot; the plant offsets readily, forming multi-headed clumps over time.

planting.note: Mount on bark or a shaded tree branch in dappled light to partial shade; needs no soil. Needle airplant is a small Florida and Gulf Coast native that forms grassy clumps and is very forgiving of humid, still garden air.

directions: Mount on bark, a shaded branch, or grow loose in a hanging basket in dappled sun to partial shade. Tillandsia setacea is a slender, grass-like air plant native to Florida and the coastal Gulf South, forming tufts of thin, wiry, needle-like gray-green leaves that resemble a small clump of grass more than a typical bromeliad. Thin, wand-like flower spikes bear small violet flowers in late summer to fall. It grows naturally in humid, shaded hammocks and readily clumps into dense colonies through offsets, making it an easy, low-maintenance native choice for mounted or hanging display in shaded Gulf Coast gardens. Mist or dunk two to three times weekly in warm months, tapering off in winter, and ensure good air movement so the fine foliage dries within a few hours after watering.

planting.note: Mount on bark or a shaded tree branch in dappled light; needs no soil. Named for botanist William Bartram, this Florida and Gulf South native forms narrow, quill-like clumps and clumps readily in humid shade gardens.

directions: Mount on bark or a shaded branch in dappled sun to partial shade, or grow loose in a hanging basket. Tillandsia bartramii is a Florida and Gulf Coast native air plant closely related to T. setacea, distinguished by its stiffer, more erect, quill-like gray-green leaves radiating from a central point. Slender flower spikes carry small violet-blue blooms, typically in summer. Like other native clump-forming tillandsias, it thrives in the humid, still air of a shaded Gulf Coast garden and multiplies readily by offsets to form dense colonies over a few seasons. Water by misting or dunking two to three times a week during the growing season, allow to dry within a few hours, and reduce watering in winter to avoid rot in cool, damp conditions.

planting.note: Mount on bark, driftwood, or grow loose in bright indirect to gentle direct light; needs no soil. Silver star airplant is a slow-growing, fine-textured species best kept as a protected patio or indoor specimen in Gulf Coast zone 9a rather than a permanent outdoor mount.

directions: Mount on bark or driftwood, or display loose in a dish, in bright indirect to gentle direct morning light. Tillandsia argentea is a small Central American species with an almost bulbous base that tapers into extremely fine, wiry, silvery leaves radiating outward in a starburst pattern, giving the plant its common name. Mature specimens send up a slender red-bracted flower spike with small violet blooms. Its fine leaf structure sheds water and dries quickly, but also means it is less forgiving of neglect than fatter-leaved species and benefits from more frequent misting in dry indoor air. In Gulf Coast gardens it is best grown as a container or hanging specimen brought under cover during freezes rather than left as a permanent outdoor mount. Water by dunking two to three times weekly in the growing season, shaking off excess water so it dries within a few hours.
